items.text: WTI crude surged 1.8% to $86.48/bbl and Brent climbed 3.0% to $95.29 as geopolitical tensions persist. Middle East conflict risks continue to anchor oil prices, threatening consumer purchasing power and adding cost-push pressure that may complicate Fed rate-cut decisions.

Payrolls dropped unexpectedly by 23K in July, but unemployment held at 4.1% and claims remain subdued at 206K. The deterioration is real—services employment contracted in July—signaling early labor softening that elevates recession risk and constrains credit demand, especially in cyclical sectors.

Headline CPI moderated to 3.3% YoY (from 3.46%) and core to 2.47% (from 2.57%), while PCE core sits at 3.29%. Despite easing headline inflation, sticky core and energy-driven tail risks remain; one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3% in early August, signaling consumer anxiety.

Fed funds steady at 3.75%; 10Y TSY at 4.65% (+2bps) and 2Y at 4.19% (+4bps) as curve flattens to 50bp. ECB hold at 2.25% deposit rate since June; no near-term cuts expected. Tight policy and sticky inflation keep real rates elevated, pressuring leveraged credit and refinance-sensitive sectors.

HY OAS widened 5bp to 275, IG OAS rose 1bp to 82, and CCC OAS spiked 17bp to 1035—deepening stress in lower-rated credits. Spread widening despite stable rates signals credit deterioration, not Fed shift; distress is broadening beyond isolated pockets into BB/B territory.

GDPNow jumped to 4.03% (from 1.54%) on strong services momentum, but underlying consumption is slowing. July retail sales fell 0.6% MoM (worst since May 2025), housing starts collapsed 12.5% YoY to 1.24M, and Q2 GDP came in at just 1.5% (from 2.1% prior). Growth is soft and decelerating.

UMich sentiment plunged to 51.0 in early August (from 55.2 in July, consensus 54.5), with expectations for business conditions down 11% near-term and 17% long-term. Existing home sales slid to 4.06M SAAR (from 4.13M), mortgage rates at 6.65%; consumer purchasing power eroding despite moderating inflation.

themeCards.title: Payroll Shock—Early Labor Deterioration
themeCards.statusLine: July nonfarm payrolls fell 23K, an unexpected reversal after months of solid gains. Services employment contracted (ISM Services employment back to 47.4 in July), signaling broad labor softening.
themeCards.relevance: For credit investors, labor weakness undermines credit quality in consumer-sensitive sectors and signals margin compression ahead. Rising unemployment risk and payroll volatility feed recession fears, pressuring valuations across leveraged issuers and widening spreads.

themeCards.title: Consumer Sentiment Cliff—August Reversion
themeCards.statusLine: UMich sentiment crashed to 51.0 in early August from 55.2 in July, missing consensus of 54.5. Consumers now expect rising inflation (4.3% one-year), with only 8% expecting income growth to beat price increases.
themeCards.relevance: Sentiment collapse signals demand destruction risk, especially among lower-income households. For credit investors, this threatens retail, autos, and consumer services fundamentals; risk of rising delinquencies if spending deteriorates further.

themeCards.title: China Manufacturing Contraction—Demand Reset
themeCards.statusLine: NBS Manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2 in July from 50.3 in June, indicating contraction for three consecutive months. Production, new orders, and exports all contracted; employment remains under pressure.
themeCards.relevance: China slowdown pressures export-heavy US sectors (autos, tech, industrials) and reduces EM demand. For special situations, watch for distress in supply-chain-exposed credits; tight liquidity and rising refinance risk in China-exposed corporates.

themeCards.title: Retail Sales Momentum Broken—Consumer Retrenchment
themeCards.statusLine: July retail sales fell 0.6% MoM (biggest drop since May 2025), well below +0.1% consensus. Nonstore retail (e-commerce) collapsed 2.2%; even ex-autos/gas, spending flatlined. YoY growth decelerated to 5.0% from 6.9% in May.
themeCards.relevance: Retail weakness is real, not just seasonal. Credit spreads in retail, restaurants, and consumer discretionary are vulnerable if spending continues to stall. Refinance stress and covenant tightness likely to accelerate in H2 2026.

themeCards.title: Curve Flattening with Spread Widening—Pressure Intensifying
themeCards.statusLine: 2-10 curve compressed to 50bp (from 51bp). Meanwhile, HY OAS jumped to 275 (from 270), IG OAS to 82 (from 81), and CCC OAS to 1035 (from 1018)—spreads widening despite stable rates.
themeCards.relevance: Flattening + widening is a classic credit deterioration signal: tighter policy, slowing growth, and rising idiosyncratic risk. Term premium compression combined with falling realized returns creates distressed-debt and restructuring opportunities, but systemic risk if widening accelerates.

themeCards.title: Energy Price Shock—Cost Inflation Resurging
themeCards.statusLine: WTI jumped 1.8% to $86.48 and Brent 3.0% to $95.29 on Middle East geopolitical tensions. Oil-sensitive sectors face renewed input cost pressures; airline, transport, and chemical spreads at risk.
themeCards.relevance: Energy spike threatens to re-ignite inflation expectations and derail consumer spending further. For credit investors, watch leverage in energy-intensive sectors; refiners have margin compression risk, while consumer services face margin squeeze if energy stays elevated.

regime.label: Late-cycle Deceleration
regime.detail: Spreading labor weakness, collapsing consumer sentiment, energy-driven cost pressure, widening credit spreads despite stable rates, and slowing consumption point to growth cliff and rising systemic credit risk.
